title: 22. Interview: Design Pastebin
summary: Interview Q&A for Design Pastebin — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Design Pastebin interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Step 6: Trade-offs & Interview Q&A (5 min)
sections.body:
### Trade-offs Discussed
- **Inline vs S3 for bodies**: inline (≤ 4 KB) saves a round-trip on read but bloats DynamoDB item size; S3 is cheaper at scale but adds 20-50 ms latency. We pick a 4 KB threshold based on observed read latency vs cost curves.
- **Server-side vs client-side password decryption**: server-side is simpler (works with curl, browser) but server briefly sees plaintext. Client-side (WebCrypto) is more secure but breaks non-browser clients. We pick server-side with TLS-only transport.
- **Pre-render vs on-demand highlighting**: pre-rendering all pastes wastes CPU on never-viewed pastes. On-demand (lazy) means the first viewer waits. We pick lazy + background pre-warm for top-100 trending pastes.
- **DynamoDB vs PostgreSQL for metadata**: DynamoDB scales without ops but loses relational queries (joins on owner/tags). PostgreSQL/Citus is ops-heavy but flexible. We pick DynamoDB for scale + a separate PG for accounts.
- **Full-text search scope**: indexing all pastes (including private) is a privacy risk; indexing only public loses the "search my pastes" feature. We pick: public pastes indexed globally; private pastes indexed per-user with row-level security.

### Conceptual Interview Questions

### Q1. Why is Pastebin read-heavy, and how does that shape the architecture?
**Answer:** The 50:1 read:write ratio comes from human behavior: a developer writes a paste once and shares the link with a team, a forum, or social media — dozens to thousands of viewers per paste. Power-law distribution amplifies this: top 1% of pastes (Stack Overflow answers, viral tweets) get 80% of total views. This shapes the architecture toward caching: CDN edge (10 min TTL) + Redis cluster (5 min TTL) absorb 90%+ of reads; the metadata DB and S3 see only the residual. Writes are simple and infrequent — even a single DynamoDB partition can absorb them. The asymmetry also means we optimize for read latency (p99 < 100 ms) more than write latency, and we cache aggressively at the edge.
**Visual:**
```
Writes (5M/day)  Reads (250M/day)
   |                |
   v                v
   DB              CDN (70%) -> Redis (20%) -> DB (10%)
```

### Q2. Why store small pastes inline in DynamoDB instead of always using S3?
**Answer:** Two reasons. (1) Latency: an inline read is a single DynamoDB GetItem (~5 ms), vs DynamoDB + S3 GetObject (~25 ms). For a 2 KB paste viewed 1 000 times, that's 20 s of latency saved per paste. (2) Cost: DynamoDB charges per KB stored (~$0.25/GB/month) vs S3 (~$0.023/GB/month) — S3 is 10× cheaper, but for small items the per-request cost ($0.0004 per 1 000 GET) dominates and DynamoDB's per-RCU pricing is comparable. The crossover is around 4 KB: above that, S3's cheaper storage outweighs its extra latency. We make the threshold configurable and tune based on observed cost/latency curves.
**Visual:**
```
paste size:
  0-4 KB    -> DynamoDB inline (1 hop, ~5ms)
  4 KB-50MB -> S3 (2 hops, ~25ms, 10x cheaper storage)
```

### Q3. How does syntax highlighting work at scale, and why is it lazy?
**Answer:** Highlighting 5 M pastes/day eagerly would burn CPU: Pygments takes ~100 ms per 10 KB paste → 5 M × 100 ms = 500 000 s of CPU/day = 6 CPU-cores continuously. But only ~10% of pastes are ever viewed, and most views are concentrated on the top 1% — so eager highlighting wastes 90% of the work. Lazy highlighting: on first view, the view service publishes a `highlight-requested` event to Kafka; a worker pool runs Pygments with a 5 s timeout (large pastes fall back to plain `<pre>`), writes HTML to Redis (5 min TTL) and S3 (long-term). Subsequent views serve from cache. Trending pastes (top 100 by view rate) get pre-warmed by a Flink job. Trade-off: the first viewer waits ~100 ms longer; everyone else sees instant HTML.
**Visual:**
```
View #1:  GET /{id} -> DB -> publish highlight event -> return plain <pre>
                                   |
                            Highlight worker (Pygments)
                                   |
                            Redis + S3 (cached HTML)
View #2+: GET /{id} -> Redis hit -> return HTML (instant)
```

### Q4. How does password protection work without the server being able to read all pastes?
**Answer:** We use envelope encryption. When a user creates a password-protected paste, the server derives a 256-bit key from the password using PBKDF2 (100 k iterations + per-paste salt), encrypts the body with AES-256-GCM, and stores only the ciphertext + salt + nonce. The password itself is never stored — only a SHA-256 hash for fast verification. On view, the client posts the password, the server re-derives the key, decrypts, and returns plaintext. The server briefly sees plaintext in memory (unavoidable for browser/curl clients). For stronger guarantees, client-side decryption via WebCrypto API lets the server never see plaintext — but breaks non-browser clients. Trade-off: server-side is simpler and universal; client-side is more secure but limits the API surface.
**Visual:**
```
Create: password -> PBKDF2 -> key -> AES-GCM(body) -> store {ct, salt, nonce}
View:   password -> PBKDF2 -> key -> AES-GCM^-1(ct) -> plaintext
Server stores: {salt, nonce, ciphertext, sha256(password)[:32]}
```

### Q5. How do you handle expiration without a costly cron job scanning the whole DB?
**Answer:** DynamoDB TTL is the primary mechanism — set `ttl_epoch` as a TTL attribute and AWS deletes the item within 48 h of the timestamp at no extra cost. The 48 h window is too loose for some users, so we also do a read-time check: if `expires_at < now()`, return 410 Gone immediately and delete the row (lazy delete on read). For S3 bodies, DynamoDB Streams emit a delete event when TTL reaper runs; a Lambda consumes it and deletes the corresponding S3 object. Cache invalidation: same stream triggers Redis DEL. For "exact" expiration (premium feature), a Redis sorted set with `expires_at` as score can be polled every second — but this is only used for high-value customers; the default is the 48 h window.
**Visual:**
```
expires_at = T + 1h
  |
  +--> TTL attribute set in DynamoDB
  +--> Read-time check: if now > expires_at -> 410 Gone, lazy delete
  +--> DynamoDB TTL reaper (within 48h) -> Streams event
  +--> Lambda -> delete S3 body, Redis DEL, OpenSearch delete
```

### Q6. Why use OpenSearch for full-text search instead of PostgreSQL FTS?
**Answer:** PostgreSQL FTS works fine up to ~10 M rows but starts to degrade at 100 M+ — index rebuilds are slow, ranking quality is poor, and sharding requires Citus or manual partitioning. OpenSearch is purpose-built for inverted-index search: it scales horizontally (100+ nodes), supports analyzers per language (e.g., CJK tokenizer for Chinese code comments), and offers advanced ranking (BM25, function_score for time-decay). For Pastebin at 150 M+ active pastes, OpenSearch is the right choice. Trade-off: OpenSearch is ops-heavy (JVM tuning, index lifecycle management, ~3× memory overhead) and adds eventual consistency (5 s lag for new pastes). We accept that for the much better search relevance and scale.
**Visual:**
```
Postgres FTS:  10M rows -> OK, 100M+ -> slow ranking, hard to shard
OpenSearch:    150M+ rows -> horizontal scale, BM25, language analyzers
                trade-off: ops overhead, 5s indexing lag
```

### Q7. How does the archival lifecycle work, and what's the cost impact?
**Answer:** S3 lifecycle policies automate tiered storage. A new paste body lands in S3 Standard ($0.023/GB/month). After 90 days untouched, it transitions to S3 Infrequent Access ($0.0125/GB, 40% savings). After 1 year, to Glacier Deep Archive ($0.00099/GB, 95% savings). After 3 years, delete. For a paste untouched for 2 years, cost drops from $0.55/GB over the period (Standard) to $0.04/GB (Glacier) — 14× cheaper. Trade-off: Glacier restore takes 12 hours; if a user views an archived paste, we serve a "restoring, check back in 12 h" page and trigger expedited restore ($0.03/GB, 1-5 min). The DynamoDB metadata row stays put (small) so the link still resolves to the restore prompt. Net: 91 TB over 5 years costs ~$270/month instead of $2 700/month.
**Visual:**
```
S3 Standard ($0.023/GB) --90d--> S3 IA ($0.0125) --1y--> Glacier ($0.001) --3y--> Delete
                                                                          ^
                                                                          |
                                                          (12h restore on access)
```

### Scenario-Based Interview Questions

### Q1. A user reports their paste was deleted but they didn't delete it — how do you investigate?
**Answer:** First, check the paste ID against DynamoDB. If the row is gone, query CloudTrail / audit log for `DeleteItem` calls on that key — was it a TTL delete (reaper) or an explicit `DELETE /api/v1/pastes/{id}` call? If TTL: check `expires_at` vs `created_at` — did the user pick a short TTL by mistake? Pastebin's default is 1 month; many users forget. If explicit delete: check the auth context — was it the owner (legitimate) or an abuse report action? Pastebin has a "report paste" flow that auto-deletes confirmed abuse. If neither, check DynamoDB Streams history — Streams retain 24 h of changes; if the delete was within 24 h, the record shows who/what triggered it. Finally, check S3 — bodies may persist after DynamoDB deletion (lifecycle lag), so partial recovery is possible. Restore: re-insert metadata row pointing to existing S3 key. Postmortem: add a "soft delete" 30-day grace period for pro users.
**Visual:**
```
paste gone?
  |
  +-- DynamoDB GetItem -> exists? no
  +-- CloudTrail: DeleteItem? -> TTL or explicit?
  +-- DynamoDB Streams (24h): who/what deleted?
  +-- S3 body still there? -> partial recovery possible
  +-- Audit: abuse report? owner action? TTL mistake?
```

### Q2. A viral paste is getting 200 k views/min — what breaks first?
**Answer:** Layer by layer. (1) CDN edge: handles 80% = 160 k/min easily, no issue. (2) Redis cluster: 18% = 36 k/min — a 6-shard Redis Cluster sustains 240 k ops/s, so fine. (3) DynamoDB: 2% = 4 k/min = ~67 QPS on one partition — well under the 3 000 RCU partition limit. (4) Bandwidth: 200 k × 10 KB = 2 GB/min egress — at the API tier we'd hit EC2 instance bandwidth caps (~5 Gbps on m5.4xlarge), so we'd need to scale out. (5) View counter: every view publishes a Kafka event → 200 k events/min = 3 333/s — Kafka handles it, but Flink incremental update to DynamoDB every 5 s means 16 M increments/batch — needs `UpdateItem` with batched counter. (6) Highlight worker: only runs once for first view, no issue. Real bottleneck: egress bandwidth and Kafka consumer lag on the analytics pipeline. Mitigation: pre-warm CDN with longer TTL, batch view counters.
**Visual:**
```
200k views/min
  | 80% CDN (160k/min)        -- fine
  | 18% Redis (36k/min)       -- fine
  | 2% DynamoDB (4k/min=67QPS)-- fine
  +-- egress 2GB/min          -- scale out API tier
  +-- Kafka 3.3k events/s     -- batch counters
```

### Q3. A developer pastes 100 MB of log output and the system returns 500. What happened?
**Answer:** Likely the request hit multiple limits. (1) API Gateway body size limit (default 10 MB on AWS, configurable up to 10 MB hard cap) — the request was rejected before reaching the service. (2) Lambda function timeout if using serverless path. (3) Application-level: if we did receive it, writing 100 MB to S3 is fine (~1 s), but the synchronous metadata write + Kafka event might block the request thread. Fix: (a) Raise API Gateway limit to 50 MB for pro users, reject free-tier > 2 MB with 413 Payload Too Large. (b) Stream large uploads directly to S3 via presigned URL — client uploads to S3, then calls `POST /pastes {s3_key, ...}` to register metadata. (c) Async metadata write with a 202 Accepted response. (d) For huge pastes, suggest splitting or using a dedicated log-sharing service like Datadog.
**Visual:**
```
Client -> 100 MB body
  |
  +--> API Gateway: 10 MB default -> 413 (raise to 50MB for pro)
  +--> Use presigned S3 upload:
        Client -> PUT S3 (presigned URL) -> returns s3_key
        Client -> POST /pastes {s3_key, language, ttl} -> 202 Accepted
```

### Q4. Pastes containing secrets (AWS keys, API tokens) keep getting leaked — how do you prevent this?
**Answer:** Multi-layer defense. (1) **Synchronous secret scanner** in the create path: scan paste content against regex patterns for AWS access keys (`AKIA...`), Slack tokens (`xoxb-...`), GitHub tokens (`ghp_...`), private keys (`-----BEGIN ... PRIVATE KEY-----`), etc. ~50 ms latency. (2) **Integration with Have I Been Pwned / GitHub's secret scanning API**: cross-reference detected tokens against known-leaked databases. (3) **User warning**: on detection, show a warning modal "We detected what looks like an AWS access key — are you sure you want to publish this?" with a "publish anyway" override. (4) **Auto-expire**: high-confidence secret detections force `visibility=private` and `ttl=1h`. (5) **Auto-report**: confirmed AWS keys → forward to AWS abuse team (they rotate within hours). (6) **Admin tooling**: a dashboard for security team to bulk-quarantine pastes with detected secrets. Real-world: GitHub does exactly this and notifies the AWS account owner.
**Visual:**
```
POST /pastes {content}
  |
  +--> regex scan (50ms): AWS keys? Slack? GitHub? private keys?
  +--> if found:
        +--> warning modal -> user confirms
        +--> force visibility=private, ttl=1h
        +--> AWS key? -> notify AWS abuse team (auto-rotate)
        +--> log to security dashboard
```

### Q5. The full-text search index is 5 minutes behind — users complain they can't find their just-created paste. How do you fix this?
**Answer:** Two paths. (1) **Reduce indexing lag**: increase OpenSearch indexing parallelism (more consumer pods on the `paste-events` topic), use bulk indexing API (batch 100 events per request), reduce refresh interval from default 1 s to 5 s during high write periods (fewer segments, faster indexing). Target: < 30 s lag. (2) **Workaround for fresh pastes**: add a "recently created by me" page that queries DynamoDB GSI `pastes_by_owner` directly (no search lag — instant). The search bar can fall back to this for queries that look like paste IDs or titles. (3) **Hybrid search**: for queries that match a paste ID exactly, skip OpenSearch and go straight to DynamoDB. (4) **Communicate**: show a "indexing..." badge on freshly-created pastes so users know it's expected. Long-term: consider a faster search backend (Manticore, Typesense) for sub-second indexing, or move to a CQRS pattern with a separate search-optimized store updated via CDC.
**Visual:**
```
Solution A: reduce lag (target <30s)
  +--> more consumers, bulk indexing, refresh_interval=5s
Solution B: workaround
  +--> "My recent pastes" page -> DynamoDB GSI (instant)
  +--> exact paste ID match -> skip OpenSearch, go to DynamoDB
Solution C: communicate
  +--> "Indexing..." badge on fresh pastes
```

### Q6. The CDN is caching a paste that the owner just edited (pro feature). How do you invalidate it?
**Answer:** Three layers to invalidate. (1) **CDN edge cache**: CloudFront supports cache invalidation by path (`/abc123`), but it costs $0.005 per path after the first 1 000/month — expensive at scale. Better: use versioned URLs (`/abc123?v=2`) and bump the version on edit — old cache entries naturally expire. Or use CloudFront's managed invalidation via Lambda@Edge on `PATCH /api/v1/pastes/{id}`. (2) **Redis cluster**: `DEL paste:{id}:html` and `paste:{id}:raw`. (3) **S3 rendered HTML object**: overwrite `s3://rendered/ab/abc123.html` with new content (S3 is read-after-write consistent as of Dec 2020). (4) **OpenSearch**: update the document — OpenSearch is near-real-time (1 s refresh). The versioning approach is cleanest: every edit bumps `version` and the URL becomes `/abc123?v=2`, which is a new cache key — no invalidation needed. Old links still resolve to v1 (or redirect to latest, configurable).
**Visual:**
```
Edit paste abc123:
  Option A (invalidation):
    PATCH -> bump version -> invalidate CDN path /abc123 -> DEL Redis -> overwrite S3 -> update OpenSearch
  Option B (versioned URL, preferred):
    PATCH -> bump version -> URL becomes /abc123?v=2
    Old /abc123 cache naturally expires (TTL 10min)
    New /abc123?v=2 is a fresh cache key
```

### Q7. You're asked to add a "fork this paste" feature (à la GitHub Gist). How do you design it?
**Answer:** Fork = copy a paste into a new paste owned by the forker, with a reference to the original. Data model: add `forked_from` field to the paste metadata. On fork: (1) `POST /api/v1/pastes/{id}/fork` — authenticate user, fetch original paste (resolve password if private + user has access), create a new paste with `owner_id = current_user`, `forked_from = original_id`, `forked_at = now`. (2) Copy body: if inline, just copy the field; if S3, do an S3 server-side copy (no bandwidth cost) to a new key. (3) Increment `fork_count` on original (async via Kafka). (4) UI: show "Forked from {original_url}" on the forked paste's page. (5) Network graph: a `forks` GSI on `forked_from` enables "X people forked this" UI. Trade-off: do we copy or reference? Copy is simpler and decouples forks from original deletions; reference saves storage but breaks if original is deleted. We pick copy for resilience. Real-world: GitHub Gist copies the content on fork.
**Visual:**
```
POST /pastes/abc123/fork
  |
  +--> fetch original (auth check)
  +--> new paste_id = snowflake.next()
  +--> S3 server-side copy: ab/abc123.txt -> cd/cdef45.txt
  +--> DynamoDB PutItem: {paste_id: cdef45, owner: current_user,
                         forked_from: abc123, forked_at: now}
  +--> Kafka event -> incr fork_count on abc123
  +--> UI: "Forked from paste.example/abc123"
```
